4 # # LSTM Training
5 # This notebook can be used to train an LSTM for text classification and generate predictions for the kaggle competition found [here](https://www.kaggle.com/c/quora-insincere-questions-classification).

39 # # 1. EDA
40 # The following code will perform basic EDA to gain an understanding of the dataset and perhaps inspire the design of the neural network.
41 #
42 # Note: Section 1 is not required for the rest of the notebook and may be skipped if desired.
43 
44 # ## 1.1 Sentiment Analysis
45 # This subsection analyzes each question using the NLTK sentiment analyzer. The goal is to determine whether the sincere and insincere questions have a significant difference in sentiment.
46 #
47 # Note: The sentiment analyis takes about 3 minutes to run on my machine. Tips are welcome on how to increase the speed of this operation!
48

53 import nltk
54 nltk.download('vader_lexicon')
55 from nltk.sentiment.vader import SentimentIntensityAnalyzer
56 
57 # Initialize the sentiment analyzer and define the sentiment extraction function
58 sid = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer()
59 def extract_sentiment(text):
60     scores = sid.polarity_scores(text)
61     return scores['compound']

160 # # 2. Data Preparation
161 # This section of the notebook is devoted to preprocessing the raw data into a form that the neural network can understand.
162 
163 # In[ ]:
164 
165 
166 # Extract the training data and corresponding labels
167 text = train_df['question_text'].fillna('unk').values
168 labels = train_df['target'].values
169 
170 # Split into training and validation sets by making use of the scikit-learn
171 # function train_test_split
172 X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(text, labels,\
173                                                   test_size=0.2)
174 
175 
176 # ## 2.1 Create Word Embedding Matrix
177 # The code in this section will identify the most commonly occurring words in the dataset. Then, it will extract the vectors for each one of these words from the GloVe pretrained word embedding and place them in an embedding layer matrix. This embedding layer will serve as the first layer of the neural network.
178 #
179 # Read more about GloVe word embeddings [here](https://nlp.stanford.edu/projects/glove/).
180 #
181 # Note that other word embeddings are also available for this competition, however glove was chosen for this notebook.
182 
183 # In[ ]:
184 
185 
186 embed_size = 300 # Size of each word vector
187 max_words = 50000 # how many unique words to use (i.e num rows in embedding vector)
188 maxlen = 100 # max number of words in a question to use
189 
190 
191 # In[ ]:
192 
193 
194 ## Tokenize the sentences
195 tokenizer = Tokenizer(num_words=max_words)
196 tokenizer.fit_on_texts(list(X_train))
197 
198 # The tokenizer will assign an integer value to each word in the dictionary
199 # and then convert each string of words into a list of integer values
200 X_train = tokenizer.texts_to_sequences(X_train)
201 X_val = tokenizer.texts_to_sequences(X_val)
202 
203 word_index = tokenizer.word_index
204 print(('The word index consists of {} unique tokens.'.format(len(word_index))))
205 
206 ## Pad the sentences
207 X_train = pad_sequences(X_train, maxlen=maxlen)
208 X_val = pad_sequences(X_val, maxlen=maxlen)
209 
210 
211 # In[ ]:
212 
213 
214 # Create the embedding dictionary from the word embedding file
215 embedding_dict = {}
216 filename = os.path.join('../input/embeddings/', 'glove.840B.300d/glove.840B.300d.txt')
217 with open(filename) as f:
218     for line in f:
219         line = line.split()
220         token = line[0]
221         try:
222             coefs = np.asarray(line[1:], dtype='float32')
223             embedding_dict[token] = coefs
224         except:
225             pass
226 print(('The embedding dictionary has {} items'.format(len(embedding_dict))))
227 
228 
229 # In[ ]:
230 
231 
232 # Create the embedding layer weight matrix
233 embed_mat = np.zeros(shape=[max_words, embed_size])
234 for word, idx in list(word_index.items()):
235     # Word index is ordered from most frequent to least frequent
236     # Ignore words that occur less frequently
237     if idx >= max_words: continue
238     vector = embedding_dict.get(word)
239     if vector is not None:
240         embed_mat[idx] = vector
241 
242 
243 # # 3. Neural Network Training
244 # This network configuration uses the pretrained GloVe embedding layer as the first layer of the network. This is followed by a bidirectional LSTM and then pooling layer. Finally, there are 2 dense layers leading to the final prediction. Feel free to modify network parameters and architecture. This is merely a starting point that provides adequate results.
245 
246 # In[ ]:
247 
248 
249 def create_lstm():
250     input = Input(shape=(maxlen,))
251 
252     # Embedding layer has fixed weights, so set 'trainable' to False
253     x = Embedding(max_words, embed_size, weights=[embed_mat], trainable=False)(input)
254     x = Bidirectional(CuDNNLSTM(64, return_sequences=True))(x)
255     x = GlobalMaxPool1D()(x)
256     x = Dense(16, activation="relu")(x)
257     x = Dropout(0.2)(x)
258     x = Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")(x)
259     model = Model(inputs=input, outputs=x)
260     model.compile(loss='binary_crossentropy', optimizer='adam', metrics=['accuracy'])
261     print((model.summary()))
262 
263     return model
264 
265 
266 # In[ ]:
267 
268 
269 # Create and train network
270 lstm = create_lstm()
271 lstm.fit(X_train, y_train, validation_data=(X_val, y_val), epochs=3, batch_size=512)

10 # ## Workflow stages

15 # 2. Acquire training and testing data.
16 # 3. Wrangle, prepare, cleanse the data.
17 # 4. Analyze, identify patterns, and explore the data.

20 # 7. Supply or submit the results.

22 # The workflow indicates general sequence of how each stage may follow the other. However there are use cases with exceptions.

24 # - We may combine mulitple workflow stages. We may analyze by visualizing data.
25 # - Perform a stage earlier than indicated. We may analyze data before and after wrangling.
26 # - Perform a stage multiple times in our workflow. Visualize stage may be used multiple times.
27 # - Drop a stage altogether. We may not need supply stage to productize or service enable our dataset for a competition.

30 # ## Question and problem definition
31 #
32 # Competition sites like Kaggle define the problem to solve or questions to ask while providing the datasets for training your data science model and testing the model results against a test dataset. The question or problem definition for Titanic Survival competition is [described here at Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/c/titanic).
33 #
34 # > Knowing from a training set of samples listing passengers who survived or did not survive the Titanic disaster, can our model determine based on a given test dataset not containing the survival information, if these passengers in the test dataset survived or not.
35 #
36 # We may also want to develop some early understanding about the domain of our problem. This is described on the [Kaggle competition description page here](https://www.kaggle.com/c/titanic). Here are the highlights to note.
37 #
38 # - On April 15, 1912, during her maiden voyage, the Titanic sank after colliding with an iceberg, killing 1502 out of 2224 passengers and crew. Translated 32% survival rate.
39 # - One of the reasons that the shipwreck led to such loss of life was that there were not enough lifeboats for the passengers and crew.
40 # - Although there was some element of luck involved in surviving the sinking, some groups of people were more likely to survive than others, such as women, children, and the upper-class.
41 #
42 # ## Workflow goals
43 #
44 # The data science solutions workflow solves for seven major goals.
45 #
46 # **Classifying.** We may want to classify or categorize our samples. We may also want to understand the implications or correlation of different classes with our solution goal.
47 #
48 # **Correlating.** One can approach the problem based on available features within the training dataset. Which features within the dataset contribute significantly to our solution goal? Statistically speaking is there a [correlation](https://en.wikiversity.org/wiki/Correlation) among a feature and solution goal? As the feature values change does the solution state change as well, and visa-versa? This can be tested both for numerical and categorical features in the given dataset. We may also want to determine correlation among features other than survival for subsequent goals and workflow stages. Correlating certain features may help in creating, completing, or correcting features.
49 #
50 # **Converting.** For modeling stage, one needs to prepare the data. Depending on the choice of model algorithm one may require all features to be converted to numerical equivalent values. So for instance converting text categorical values to numeric values.
51 #
52 # **Completing.** Data preparation may also require us to estimate any missing values within a feature. Model algorithms may work best when there are no missing values.
53 #
54 # **Correcting.** We may also analyze the given training dataset for errors or possibly innacurate values within features and try to corrent these values or exclude the samples containing the errors. One way to do this is to detect any outliers among our samples or features. We may also completely discard a feature if it is not contribting to the analysis or may significantly skew the results.
55 #
56 # **Creating.** Can we create new features based on an existing feature or a set of features, such that the new feature follows the correlation, conversion, completeness goals.

434 def DfPrepPipeline(df_predict,df_train_Cols,minVec,maxVec):
435     # Reorder the columns
436     continuous_vars = ['Age','DailyRate','DistanceFromHome','HourlyRate',
437                   'MonthlyIncome','MonthlyRate','NumCompaniesWorked',
438                   'PercentSalaryHike','TotalWorkingYears','TrainingTimesLastYear',
439                   'YearsAtCompany','YearsInCurrentRole','YearsSinceLastPromotion',
440                   'YearsWithCurrManager']
441     cat_vars =  ['Gender','OverTime','BusinessTravel','JobRole','Department',
442             'MaritalStatus','EducationField','Education','EnvironmentSatisfaction'
443             ,'JobInvolvement','JobLevel','JobSatisfaction',
444            'PerformanceRating','RelationshipSatisfaction','StockOptionLevel','WorkLifeBalance']
445     df_predict = df_predict[['Attrition'] + continuous_vars + cat_vars]
446     """One hot encode the categorical variables
447     lst = ['Gender','OverTime','BusinessTravel','JobRole','Department',
448             'MaritalStatus','EducationField','Education','EnvironmentSatisfaction'
449             ,'JobInvolvement','JobLevel','JobSatisfaction',
450            'PerformanceRating','RelationshipSatisfaction','StockOptionLevel','WorkLifeBalance']
451     remove = list()
452     for i in lst:
453         for j in df_predict[i].unique():
454             df_predict[i+'_'+j] = np.where(df_predict[i] == j,1,-1)
455         remove.append(i)
456     df_predict = df_predict.drop(remove, axis=1)
457     """
458     # Ensure that all one hot encoded variables that appear in the train data appear in the subsequent data
459     L = list(set(df_train_Cols) - set(df_predict.columns))
460     for l in L:
461         df_predict[str(l)] = -1
462     # MinMax scaling coontinuous variables based on min and max from the train data
463     df_predict[continuous_vars] = (df_predict[continuous_vars]-minVec)/(maxVec-minVec)
464     # Ensure that The variables are ordered in the same way as was ordered in the train set
465     df_predict = df_predict[df_train_Cols]
466     return df_predict

4 # ### Hello guys, today we will see how to predict the open stock price of APPL Stock. Wait a sec. What !! "predict the open stock price". Is that even possible?            Ofcourse not. Its impossible to predict open stock price otherwise we would all become billionaire.
5 # ### In this tutorial we will try to predict the upward and downward trends that exists in the APPL Stock Price, i.e. we are more interested in the directions taken by our predictions, rather than the closeness of their values to the real stock price.
6 #
7 # ###                                                                                                              We will not use time series forecasting, rather use Long short-term memory (LSTM) for our prediction. It performs well better than than the ARIMA model. We will design a stacked LSTM having high dimensionality.
8 #
9 # ###    We will train our LSTM model using 6 years of APPL stock price , starting from the last financial date of 2009 to last financial day of 2016. Based on the correlations captured by our model, we will try to predict the open stock price from 1st financial day of 2017 to last financial day of August 2018. Again, we won't predict the actual price but try to predict the upward and downward stock price trends.

510 # **POSITIVE CORRELATION:** If an **increase in feature A leads to increase in feature B, then they are positively correlated**. A value **1 means perfect positive correlation**.

512 # **NEGATIVE CORRELATION:** If an **increase in feature A leads to decrease in feature B, then they are negatively correlated**. A value **-1 means perfect negative correlation**.

836 # Now this seems to be very good accuracy for a classifier, but can we confirm that it will be 90% for all the new test sets that come over??. 841 # # Cross Validation
842 #
843 # Many a times, the data is imbalanced, i.e there may be a high number of class1 instances but less number of other class instances. Thus we should train and test our algorithm on each and every instance of the dataset. Then we can take an average of all the noted accuracies over the dataset.
844 #
845 # 1)The K-Fold Cross Validation works by first dividing the dataset into k-subsets.
846 #
847 # 2)Let's say we divide the dataset into (k=5) parts. We reserve 1 part for testing and train the algorithm over the 4 parts.
848 #
849 # 3)We continue the process by changing the testing part in each iteration and training the algorithm over the other parts. The accuracies and errors are then averaged to get a average accuracy of the algorithm.
850 #
851 # This is called K-Fold Cross Validation.
852 #
853 # 4)An algorithm may underfit over a dataset for some training data and sometimes also overfit the data for other training set. Thus with cross-validation, we can achieve a generalised model.

Now in the next iteration, the learner will focus more on the wrongly predicted instances or give more weight to it. Thus it will try to predict the wrong instance correctly. 4 # # Building End to End predictive models with sklearn pipelines
5 #
6 # Sklearn pipelines have been around for a while now. I always thought pipelines as a nifty feature that can take out the back forth scrolling in kernel notebooks between data cleaning, feature engineering and prediction steps, and have a single object/pipe that can take in data and give out predictions. I also found that this was a promiseland, it was not a easy task to create a practical/useful pipeline, that took in a DataFrame and gave out predictions.
7 #
8 # But now, after a revisit to the land of pipelines, I could bet you that pipelines are back in action. No, I'm serious, I bet that it's possible to acheive the most organized and concise code for a problem by adapting pipelines. I'm willing to bet my upvote on it ;)
9 
10 # I've explained every step along the way, So it should be easy to follow.
11 #
12 # **What can you expect in this notebook**
13 #
14 # **Beginner** - I've never heard of sklearn pipelines - You are in for a treat. You I'll be introduced to a new/clean/easy coding model to build predictive models
15 #
16 # **Intermediate** - I've dabbled with pipes, haven't used them end to end - I'll introduce you to new techniques that can help you use pipelines better.
17 #
18 # **Advanced** - I've wrote complex pipelines in production - I've made some cool tweaks and wrote a helper library with common transformation which you can evaluate. Let's dicuss best practices
19 
20 # ## Let's Start afresh...what are pipelines.
21 #
22 # On the outlook solution to any supervised learning problem, is to learn a set of transformations to apply to the training data so that it matches the results closely, and applying the same transformation to the future test data, to get closely matching result. This entire process is the premise of pipelines. Pipelines are objects that help to record a chain of transformer steps applied to training data, and apply the same to the test data.
23 #
24 #
25 # ![Imgur](https://i.imgur.com/tDMLxup.png)
26 #
27 # ### What are the benefits of this approach.
28 #
29 # - You are in complete control of the transformations that goes in to your final model.
30 # - The whole model right from data preprocessing to regression/classification can be pickled into a single object. No more is the trouble of remembering what features went into my best model.
31 # - When used right, reduces the lines of code drastically, this is more apparent when you start developing reusable transformers. (Exactly what I've done here)
32 # - It's data leakage proof. Here is an [interesting read](https://machinelearningmastery.com/data-leakage-machine-learning/) on this topic. This is illustrated in detail in the coming sections.
33 
34 # ## Now to the problem at hand.
35 #
36 # There are pretty awesome kernels out there that does an amazing job at feature engineering. So without going in depth on that, let's do some basic analysis of our data.

105 # ## Libraries required
106 #
107 # The base library of our pipelines is [sklearn.pipeline](http://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/pipeline.html), in addition to that we'll be requiring a few helpers to make life easier.
108 #
109 # ### [sklearn_pandas](https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/sklearn-pandas)
110 #

112 #
113 # `pip install sklearn_pandas`
114 #
115 # sklearn pipelines natively have poor support for pandas dataframe, sklearn_pandas is an effort to bridge the gap between pandas and sklearn. They have an amazingly easy documentation to their api, it took me just an hour to adapt it in my flow, I would highly encourage everyone to give it a try.

144 import numpy as np
145 from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer
146 from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin
147 from sklearn_pandas import DataFrameMapper
148 
149 class CustomImputer(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin):
150     def __init__(self, strategy='mean', filler='NA'):
151         self.strategy = strategy
152         self.fill = filler
153 
154     def fit(self, X, y=None):
155         if self.strategy in ['mean', 'median']:
156             if not all([dtype in [np.number, np.int] for dtype in X.dtypes]):
157                 raise ValueError('dtypes mismatch np.number dtype is required for ' + self.strategy)
158         if self.strategy == 'mean':
159             self.fill = X.mean()
160         elif self.strategy == 'median':
161             self.fill = X.median()
162         elif self.strategy == 'mode':
163             self.fill = X.mode().iloc[0]
164         elif self.strategy == 'fill':
165             if type(self.fill) is list and type(X) is pd.DataFrame:
166                 self.fill = dict([(cname, v) for cname, v in zip(X.columns, self.fill)])
167         return self
168 
169     def transform(self, X, y=None):
170         if self.fill is None:
171             self.fill = 'NA'
172         return X.fillna(self.fill)
173 
174 def CustomMapper(result_column='mapped_col', value_map={}, default=np.nan):
175     def mapper(X, result_column, value_map, default):
176         def colmapper(col):
177             return col.apply(lambda x: value_map.get(x, default))
178         mapped_col = X.apply(colmapper).values
179         mapped_col_names = [result_column + '_' + str(i) for i in range(mapped_col.shape[1])]
180         return pd.DataFrame(mapped_col, columns=[mapped_col_names])
181     return FunctionTransformer(
182         mapper,
183         validate=False,
184         kw_args={'result_column': result_column, 'value_map': value_map, 'default': default}
185     )

424 # ## Building Custom Transformer for Pipelines

426 # All our engineered features involves comparing if two columns equal or unequal to each other. A single transformer that does this is all we need to engineer these features to our pipeline.
427 #
428 # Let's see how to develop a custom transformer to be used in pipeline.
429 #
430 # A Transformer by definition should support the **fit()/transform()** interface. There are two ways to achieve this,
431 #
432 # * creating a class which inherits from **sklean.base.TransformerMixin** and override fit() and transform()
433 # * **sklearn.preprocessing.FunctionTransformer** can be used to transform any functions to a transformer
434 #
435 # We I'll be using the **FunctionTransformer** as it's simpler and adequete for our needs. You can check out the other method [here](https://github.com/gautham20/sklearn_pipeline_utils/blob/master/sklearn_pipeline_utils/skutils.py) in defenition of **CustomImputer**

440 from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer
441 
442 def ColumnsEqualityChecker(result_column='equality_col', inverse=False):
443     def equalityChecker(X, result_column, inverse=False):
444         def roweq(row):
445             eq = all(row.values == row.values[0])
446             return eq
447         eq = X.apply(roweq, axis=1)
448         if inverse:
449             eq = eq.apply(np.invert)
450         return pd.DataFrame(eq.values.astype(int), columns=[result_column])
451     return FunctionTransformer(
452         equalityChecker,
453         validate=False,
454         kw_args={'result_column': result_column, 'inverse': inverse}
455     )
456 
457 
458 # **ColumnsEqualityChecker** returns a FunctionTransformer that wraps the function **equalityChecker**. Any arguments to equalityChecker can be passed in kw_args of FunctionTransformer

98 def rec(y_true , y_predict):
99     '''
100     Regression Error Characteristic curve with X-axis represents deviation, and y-axis shows
101     the current accuracy under deviation, return the range of deviation, the accuracy of every
102     deviation, the area under the curve
103     '''
104     accuracy = []
105     begin = 0
106     end = 15
107     interval = 0.1
108 
109     epsilon = np.arange(begin, end, interval)
110 
111     # loop to find the accuracy for every deviation
112     for i in range(len(epsilon)):
113         count = 0
114         for j in range(len(y_true)):
115             if np.abs(y_true[j] - y_predict[j]) < epsilon[i]:
116                 count = count + 1
117 
118         accuracy.append(count/len(y_true))
119 
120     #  using Simpson's rule to calculating area-under-curve
121     area_under_curve = simps(accuracy, epsilon) / end
122 
123     return epsilon, accuracy, area_under_curve
124 
125 
126 def NLL(y_true, y_predict):
127     '''
128     defined as : −log𝑝(𝑦|𝐷,𝑥),
129     where y is the true value, D is the dataset, x represents a query point
130     '''
131     y_predict_mean = np.mean(y_predict)
132     y_predict_variance = np.var(y_predict)
133 
134     return np.log(2 * np.pi * y_predict_variance) / 2 + \
135             np.sum((y_true - y_predict_mean) ** 2) / (2 * y_predict_variance)
136 
137 
138 def mean_absolute_deviation(y_predict):
139     '''
140     the mean absolue deviation of every prediction to the prediction mean, defined as:
141     mean(abs(p - y_predict.mean() for p in y_predict))
142     '''
143     prediction_mean = np.mean(y_predict)
144     distance = np.abs(y_predict - prediction_mean)
145     return np.sum(distance) / len(y_predict)

379 #
380 # $$\frac 1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2$$

383 #
384 # $$\sqrt{\frac 1n\sum_{i=1}^n(y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}$$

386 # Comparing these metrics:
387 #

390 # - **RMSE** is even more popular than MSE, because RMSE is interpretable in the "y" units.
